     I.       INTRODUCTION

         As discussed in its Initial Brief, Scimitar Partners LP and Bar H Bar Land & Cattle Co.

(collectively, “Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve” or “ranch”) opposes route 894 proposed by

Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation

(“LCRA”) (collectively, “Joint Applicants”) as the route that best meets the Public Utility

Commission of Texas (“PUCT” or “Commission”) routing criteria. 1 Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve is concerned that certain routing links, specifically links H1 and G52, would substantially

affect ranching and preservation efforts on the ranch and require significant reductions in the area

usable on the ranch for both. The Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve, as opposed to most of the

ranches and properties affected in this proceeding, is a unique property with specific concerns that

other properties would not have in the study area. Further, this Reply Brief responds to certain

parties’ claims in support of route 894 and any other route that utilizes links H1 or G52. Lastly,

this Reply Brief will discuss alternative routes proposed by certain parties that are superior to route

894 or any other route that utilizes links H1 or G52.

         For the reasons stated above, and as will be outlined throughout this Reply Brief, Bar H

Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve urges the State Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”)

Administrative Law Judges (“ALJ”) and ultimately the PUCT Commissioners to not select route

894 or another alternative route that utilizes links H1 and G52. Further, Bar H Bar Ranch and

Nature Preserve urges the SOAH ALJs and ultimately the Commission to adopt one of the

alternative routes outlined in this Reply Brief that does not utilize links H1 or G52.




1
 Direct Testimony of Casey D. Petty, P.E. adopted by Brenda J. Perkins, Oncor Exhibit 5 (Petty/Perkins Direct) at
Bates 11-12.

                                                         3
        II.       ARGUMENT
                 A. Response to selected parties in support of route 894.


                            1. Joint Applicants

             Joint Applicants selected route 894 as the route they think best meets the appliable routing

factors outlined in the Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) and Texas Administrative Code

(“TAC”).2 However, the Joint Applicants make clear that they are required by the Commission’s

Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) application form to identify a route they think

best meets the Commission’s routing criteria, but that it is ultimately up the Commission to select

the route to construct.3 Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve appreciates the Joint Applicants

commitment to build any route selected, but Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve believes that

due to the shortened timelines to prepare the application and the vast distance that any of the

proposed alternative routes covers, that Joint Applicants did not have the time, resources, or

information necessary to make a reasoned selection. Now that the various intervenors have

provided that information to supplement what Joint Applicants provided, Bar H Bar Ranch and

Nature Preserve will show that route 894 is not a prudent selection on a number of grounds.

                                      i.    Cost

             First, the Joint Applicants simply did not have the necessary information to effectively

evaluate cost for the various routing alternatives. Joint Applicants in their initial brief claim that

“[b]ecause every route was estimated using the same methodology, the cost differences among the

routes reflect route-specific construction requirements and provide a reliable basis for



2
    Joint Applicant’s Initial Brief at 40-41 (Jun. 19, 2026).
3
    Id. at 41.

                                                                4
 distinguishing among the routes.”4 This is simply not true, and as shown by Bar H Bar Ranch and

Nature Preserve routing witness Michael D. Noonan, Joint Applicant’s significantly

underestimated the cost of right-of-way (“ROW”) acquisition for links H1 and G52 by tens of

millions of dollars.5 Mr. Noonan went on to state that he saw nowhere in the Joint Applicants’

application that mentions these extraordinary damages to the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve.6 Joint Applicant witness Corin Cooley confirmed this in cross-examination when she

admitted that the Joint Applicants did not do a per link analysis and did not take into account

unique features on a property in their cost analysis.7 Given that the distinct features of the Bar H

Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve were not factored into ROW acquisition estimates for the proposed

routes, the cost of any route, including route 894, that utilizes links H1 or G52 will be significantly

more costly than Joint Applicants have provided in their costs estimates. Further, we found no

evidence that any other property or tract of land had such a significant disparity in the estimated

cost of ROW acquisition as compared to the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve which makes

the property unique in the underestimating of costs necessary for ROW acquisition.

            This goes to show that the SOAH ALJs and the Commission should be very skeptical of

the cost information provided by Joint Applicants, especially regarding the Bar H Bar Ranch and

Nature Preserve, and not take any such information as fact. The one-size-fits-all approach when it

comes to ROW acquisition analysis that Joint Applicants employed completely ignores the

significant differences between properties in the study area. By not taking into account those

unique features of certain properties, as Ms. Cooley admitted Joint Applicants did not do, a


4
    Id. at 45.
5
    Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Initial Brief at 28-29 (Jun. 19, 2026).
6
    Id. at 29.
7
    Tr. (Jun. 08, 2026) at 232:5 – 232:14.

                                                           5
 property like the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve is evaluated on a ROW cost basis the same

as a vacant piece of land with no additional value other than land cost. Mr. Noonan pointed out the

flaws with this approach stating the ranch “operations are dependent on pristine habitat, open lands

with no interior fences, secluded pastures and water bodies for birthing new animals, and strategic

LZs for aerial helicopter operations used in game management and transfers.” 8 Further, the

construction of links H1 or G52 “would completely inhibit current operations and cause the Bar H

Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve to be unable to continue these specialized operations.” 9 Not only

this but the costs related to both fragmentation of the property into three district tracts as well as

aesthetic and view shed damages will significantly increase ROW acquisition costs and the Joint

Applicants have not taken any of this into account in their cost assessment. Further, as noted earlier

these unique features of the ranch would increase the ROW acquisition costs by tens of millions

of dollars over what the Joint Applicants estimated. Simply put, the SOAH ALJs and Commission

should be very critical of Joint Applicants’ cost estimates especially between any routes that are

within tens of millions of dollars of each other. For those reasons we urge the SOAH ALJs and

Commission to look skeptically at the cost of any route that utilizes links H1 and G52 and select a

route that does not utilize either link to avoid costs not accounted for in Joint Applicants’

application.

                               ii.    Habitable Structures

          Next, the SOAH ALJs and Commission should be skeptical of data regarding habitable

structures provided by Joint Applicants. Joint Applicants say in their initial brief that evidence of



8
 Direct Testimony of Michael D. Noonan, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Exhibit 1 (Noonan Direct) at Bates
21.
9
    Id.

                                                      6
 habitable structures “is in the record, and the Commission may weigh this evidence in evaluating

the habitable structures within proximity to each proposed route.” 10 This is only partially true and

further obfuscates the truth by implying that the Joint Applicants provided the necessary

information to evaluate habitable structures, which they did not. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve witness Michael D. Noonan identified three (3) habitable structures, all single-family

homes on the ranch, within 500-feet of link H1 that the Joint Applicants did not identify in their

application.11 This goes to the wider problem with the application and information provided by

Joint Applicants, that is, that it is simply unreliable. This is shown by the fact that on one portion

of one link, link H1, the Joint Applicants missed three (3) habitable structures and, given the

numerous links available to choose from, it becomes impossible to know how many habitable

structures they missed overall and makes accepting the figures provided by Joint Applicants

wholly unreliable. This goes to the problem that Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve identified

earlier in this Reply Brief that due to the shortened timelines and vast size of the study area that

any of the proposed routes cover, Joint Applicants simply did not have the time, resources, or

information to make a reasoned selection. For this reason, the SOAH ALJs and Commission

should look to factors other than habitable structure count, that can be reliably evaluated when

determining what route to recommend and ultimately approve in this proceeding.

                                     iii.    Environmental Integrity

            The Joint Applicants did not address environmental integrity directly in their initial brief

nor did they discuss endangered species affected by the proposed routes. However, Bar H Bar

Ranch and Nature Preserve thinks it is prudent to address environmental integrity as part of the


10
     Joint Applicant’s Initial Brief at 46 (Jun. 19, 2026).
11
     Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Exhibit 1, Noonan Direct at Bates 14.

                                                              7
 larger theme of the Joint Applicants not providing a full picture of the effects that certain routing

links would have. Like with cost and habitable structures, simply put, the Joint Applicants did not

give the SOAH ALJs or the Commission a clear enough picture to make an informed decision.

           To this point, the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve has over 30 species of animals on

the ranch that are actively taken care of by ranch staff. 12 Those include at least five (5) species that

are listed by either the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (“IUCN”) or Endangered

Species Act (“ESA”) as protected in some form. 13 The below is a list of those protected species

and their designation:


               Species                          Organization                       Protected Status

                                               IUCN Red List                    Critically Endangered
                Addax
                                                     ESA                              Endangered

               Lechwe                          IUCN Red List                        Near Threatened

                                               IUCN Red List                     Critically Endangered
            Dama Gazelle
                                                     ESA                              Endangered

           Himalayan Tahr                      IUCN Red List                       Near Threatened

                                               IUCN Red List                          Endangered
            Scimitar Oryx
                                                     ESA                              Endangered




12
  Direct Testimony of Holliday Hinckley, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Exhibit 2 (Hinckley Direct) at
Bates 37-40.
13
     Id.

                                                       8
            The Joint Applicants did not include any of the above species in their environmental

assessment.14 Further, all of this information was available to Joint Applicants through

communications with Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve as well as via direct testimony and

yet the Joint Applicants did not include this information in their environmental assessment or

update their recommendation upon learning about these species. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve thinks it is important to show the effects this oversight would have on these populations

of animals. Construction of the transmission line on links H1 or G52 will significantly affect the

Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s ability to maintain the robust species of animals it

currently has, and given that more reasonable options exist to place the transmission line, it does

not make sense to disturb such a large number of endangered and protected species that live on the

ranch.

           Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s Initial Brief15 provides great detail about additional

effects that the transmission line will have on all of the animals on the ranch including the

endangered species, and we will not rehash those arguments here. However, this goes to the

broader point of the failure of the Joint Applicants to give the SOAH ALJs and the Commission

the necessary information to make a reasoned, well-informed decision. None of the information

regarding the animals on the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve including the five (5)

endangered or protected species on the ranch was provided by Joint Applicants for the SOAH

ALJs or Commission to evaluate. Further, selection of route 894 was made without this additional

information and the Joint Applicants made no effort to update that evaluation upon learning of this




14
  Joint Applicants’ Response to Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s First Requests for Information 1-3, Bar H
Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Exhibit 4.
15
     Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Initial Brief at 13-22.

                                                           9
 additional information. This just furthers the clear theme of this proceeding in that Joint Applicants

simply did not have the time, resources, or information to make a reasoned selection.

                           2. U3 Landowners

            The U3 Landowners support selection of route 894 and generally provide an analysis as to

why it is better than one of the alternative routes, route 392, recommended by certain intervenors. 16

The top reasons that U3 Landowners claim supports selection of route 894 over route 392 are that

it costs $34,299,000 less and has 60% less habitable structures. 17 This goes to the wider theme of

this Reply Brief, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve has shown that simply relying on Joint

Applicants’ information at face value is not reasonable. Evidence in this Reply Brief has already

shown that both cost estimates and habitable structure count for route 894 are inaccurate and cut

against the two main reasons U3 Landowners provide in support of route 894 over route 392.

            Further, three separate expert witnesses in this proceeding, all with Ph.D.’s, state that link

U3 is the best place to cross the Colorado River to mitigate impacts to the river. Direct Testimony

of Dr. Mark Turnbough, Ph.D. states that only one link, link U3, crosses the Colorado River

running parallel to existing compatible ROW. 18 Dr. Andrew Sansom, Ph.D. states that link “U3

parallels existing transmission infrastructure and presents the opportunity to utilize and parallel an

existing corridor, rather than introducing an entirely new infrastructure corridor across the

Colorado River.”19 Dr. Sansom goes on to say that “utilizing Link U3 best minimizes new

environmental disturbances” for crossing the Colorado River. 20 Lastly, Dr. Joshua D. Rhodes,


16
     Initial Brief of U3 Landowners at 1-2 (Jun. 19, 2026).
17
     Id. at 2.
18
     Direct Testimony of Mark Turnbough, Ph.D., Brady Creek Intervenors Exhibit 4 at 10.
19
     Direct Testimony of Andrew Sansom, Ph.D., Brady Creek Intervenors Exhibit 3 (Sansom Direct) at 13.
20
     Id. at 16.

                                                              10
 Ph.D., argues that “[l]ink U3 crosses the Colorado River in a location that parallels existing electric

transmission infrastructure, whereas every other link that crosses the Colorado River would create

a new crossing corridor. By utilizing Link U3, the proposed transmission line would consolidate

infrastructure within an existing corridor rather than introducing a whole new crossing location.” 21

           The Colorado River is a vital river and water source in Texas and even lends its name to

one of the Joint Applicants in this proceeding. LCRA is the Lower Colorado River Authority and

as part of its mission statement notes that it manages the lower Colorado River. 22 It is odd that the

entity charged with managing and protecting the Colorado River has selected a route that further

harms the environmental and aesthetic integrity of the river by creating yet another transmission

corridor crossing. As all three doctors argue, it is a much more reasonable proposition to simply

cross the river where there is already an existing transmission line. This mitigates additional

environmental and aesthetic impacts and prevents a second, brand-new crossing of the river.

           Though Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve thinks other reasonable routes do exist,

mitigating impacts to the Colorado River is a compelling reason in support of route 392.

Ultimately, this transmission line is going to impact a lot of properties and cost relatively similar

amounts of money, but protecting one of the most important rivers in the state and the country is

a significant factor that points towards selection of route 392 and the use of link U3 to cross the

Colorado River.




21
     Direct Testimony of Joshua D. Rhodes, Ph.D., Solana Intervenors Exhibit 4 at 13.
22
     See, LCRA website (https://www.lcra.org/about/overview/).

                                                          11
                      3. Other Intervenors supporting route 894.

       By Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s count, north of 131 parties filed an initial brief

in this proceeding. That number is significantly more than could be read, comprehended, and

responded to in seven (7) calendar days. Some of those 131 initial briefs provide support for route

894 and for the most part all follow a similar theme. That is, route 894 is a reasonable balance of

cost and habitable structures and should be selected for those reasons. Without the ability to

respond to every brief that supports route 894 on those grounds, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve will respond to that argumentation generally here.

       As has already been noted in both this Reply Brief and Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve’s Initial Brief, cost estimates for link H1 alone are off by tens of millions of dollars for

ROW acquisition and any route that uses link H1, including route 894, will be significantly more

expensive than Joint Applicants have claimed. Relying on the Joint Applicants’ cost estimates in

this proceeding is simply not a reasonable or reliable way to evaluate routing options. Joint

Applicants did not have the time, resources, or information necessary to provide an accurate,

reliable cost estimate in this proceeding. Therefore, reliance on Joint Applicants’ cost estimates

alone will lead to selection of a route that does not best meet the routing criteria in both PURA and

TAC. Instead, we urge the SOAH ALJs and Commission to look to additional evidence that shows

the errors in Joint Applicants’ estimates and include that information when evaluating which route

best meets the Commission’s routing criteria.

       The same deficiencies regarding cost estimates are true of the habitable structure count

presented by Joint Applicants. As noted earlier in this Reply Brief, on only a small portion of link

H1 alone, which crosses the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve, the Joint Applicants failed to

identify three (3) habitable structures within 500-feet of the centerline of link H1. Even when



                                                 12
 presented with this failure to identify those habitable structures, Joint Applicants did not update

their habitable structure count to reflect these additional habitable structures. Therefore, it is

unreasonable to rely on the Joint Applicants’ count of habitable structures given there have been

clearly identified structures that were missed and the Joint Applicants when presented with this

clear evidence did not update the habitable structure count or contemplate whether their original

route selection was reasonable in light of this new evidence. Therefore, any party relying on the

habitable structure count provided by Joint Applicants to justify selection of route 894, will be

making said argument based upon inaccurate information. Therefore, we urge the SOAH ALJs

and the Commission to look to additional evidence which shows significantly more habitable

structures within 500-feet of the centerline of links that comprise route 894. When looking at this

additional evidence, it calls into question the reasonability of selecting route 894.

                B. Response to Commission Staff’s recommended route.

            Commission Staff has proposed route 487 as the route they believe best meets the routing

criteria outlined in PURA and TAC. Commission Staff argues that route 487 performs well on

quantitative features as compared to other routes. 23 Staff argues that route 487 compares favorably

to other routes on the following categories: (1) community values; recreational and park areas; (3)

cultural, aesthetic, and historical values; (4) environmental integrity; (5) cost; (6) use of existing

corridors; and (7) prudent avoidance.24

            However, Commission Staff witness John Poole states that he almost selected route 296

over route 487, but ultimately selected route 487.25 Mr. Poole also said that though he selected

route 487, he did not believe it was unreasonable to select 296 as the route that is constructed


23
     Commission Staff’s Initial Brief at 5-6 (Jun. 19, 2026).
24
     Id. at 12-17.
25
     Tr. (Jun. 10, 2026) at 126:4 – 126:15.

                                                            13
 related to this proceeding.26 However, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve will note that

selection of route 296 does not suffer the same fatal flaws that selection of route 894 does or that

route 487 partially does because route 296 does not use links H1 or G52. Therefore, it would not

result in the additional costs and habitable structure numbers that the other routes suffer from based

upon Joint Applicants’ incomplete analysis.

           Lastly, though Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve does prefer that a route other than

894 or 487 is selected by the Commission, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve strongly prefers

route 487 recommended by Commission Staff to route 894 recommended by Joint Applicants.

This is because route 487 only utilizes link G52 whereas route 894 utilizes both links H1 and G52.

While link G52 cuts across the northern portion of the ranch and will cause adverse impacts to

ranch operations, link H1 bisects a significant portion of the ranch running north/south and will

have substantially more devastating impacts on the ranch. While no landowner wants a

transmission line on their ranch, including Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve, the ranch would

much prefer that the transmission line be sited on link G52, if necessary, to avoid the devastating

effects that link H1 would have on the ranch. Further, the analysis provided in this Reply Brief and

in Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s Initial Brief regarding inaccurate cost analysis and

habitable structure counts is far more significant on link H1 than it is on link G52. Therefore, Bar

H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve urges the SOAH ALJs and Commissioners to select route 392,

but if not, then to select 487 over route 894 to the extent those are the final selections up for

consideration in this proceeding.




26
     Tr. (Jun. 10, 2026) at 124:12 – 124:17.

                                                 14
                 C. Response to various alternative routes that do not utilize links H1 and G52.

            Other than Commission Staff, multiple other parties offered alternative routes in this

proceeding and Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve provides limited comments on some of

those routes below.

                            1. 4K Land and Cattle Company

            The 4K Land and Cattle Company recommends that the Commission select a route in the

northern corridor including routes 74, 93, 100, 391, 392, 402, 410, 416, 589, or 592. 27 While Bar

H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve has not fully evaluated all of these routes, they would not be

opposed to selection of any of these routes to the extent the Commission finds them reasonable.

Further, as discussed earlier in this Reply Brief, all of these routes use U3 to cross the Colorado

River which is the least environmentally and aesthetically impactful on the river. Therefore,

selection of any of the routes recommended by 4K Land and Cattle Company would be the least

impactful to the Colorado River and provide additional support for a selection of one of the above

routes.

                            2. Soluna Intervenors and Brady Creek Intervenors

            Both the Soluna Intervenors28 and the Brady Creek Intervenors29 recommend that the

Commission select route 392, which was also recommended by 4K Land and Cattle Company.

Soluna Intervenors argue that selection of route 392, which utilizes link U3 to cross the Colorado

River, avoids “the creation of a new crossing corridor where none currently exists” 30 They further

argues that route 392 avoids extended pipeline parallelling, and performs favorable on cost,


27
     4K Land and Cattle Company’s Initial Brief at 27 (Jun. 19, 2026).
28
     Initial Brief of the Solana Intervenors at 17 (Jun. 19, 2026).
29
     Initial Brief of Brady Creek Intervenors at 45 (Jun. 19, 2026).
30
     Initial Brief of the Solana Intervenors at 17 (Jun. 19, 2026).

                                                              15
 habitable structures, and environmental criteria. 31 Brady Creek Intervenors argue further that route

392 parallels substantially more compatible infrastructure across the study area while route 894

instead “bisect intact, historically undeveloped ranchland with no existing compatible

infrastructure and no established corridor for high-voltage transmission.” 32

            Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve agrees with Soluna Intervenors, Brady Creek

Intervenors, and 4K Land and Cattle Company that route 392 is likely the best choice to be selected

by the Commission. First, route 392 does not utilize links H1 and G52 so is less likely to suffer

from substantial cost overruns as well as substantial undercounting of habitable structures which

route 894 suffers from. Next, it crosses the Colorado River at link U3 which parallels existing

transmission infrastructure providing the least impactful crossing of the river of any link. Lastly,

as described by Brady Creek Intervenors, route 392 is less impactful to land in the area by not

bifurcating ranches like the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve and instead following

compatible existing infrastructure. For those reasons Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve

strongly supports Soluna Intervenors, Brady Creek Intervenors, and 4K Land and Cattle

Company’s recommendation that the Commission select route 392.

                           3. Save the Lampasas

            Save the Lampasas supports the selection of either route 296 or route 572 as the route that

best meets the Commission routing criteria. 33 Save the Lampasas argues that both routes 296 and

572 perform especially well on community values, environmental integrity, impacts to parks and

recreational areas, and historical and aesthetic values.34 Further, they argue that overall both routes

     Id. at 17.
32
     Initial Brief of Brady Creek Intervenors at 45(Jun. 19, 2026).

     Save the Lampasas’s Initial Brief at 2-3 (Jun.19, 2026).
34
     Id. at 11.

                                                            16
 perform well on all of the Commission’s routing criteria and either should be selected by the

Commission.35 Though Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve has concerns that neither route uses

link U3 to cross the Colorado River, both routes are still far superior to routes 894 and route 496.

Further, neither route uses links H1 or G52 which, as has been addressed extensively in this Reply

Brief, suffer from significant cost discrepancies as well as significant undercounting of habitable

structures. While Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve ultimately thinks route 392 is the better

route selection, it agrees that selection of either route 296 or 572 is a reasonable selection that it

could support.

                            4. Cherokee Creek Partners, et. al. and Segment K13/K51 Landowners

            Cherokee Creek Partners supports selection of Cherokee Creek Route G as the route that

best meets the Commission routing criteria. 36 Cherokee Creek Partners argue that their analysis

was the only one that “undertook a systematic, quantitative and qualitative review of the alternative

routes using a consistent comparative framework.”37 Further, Cherokee Creek Partners argues that

their quartile analysis exposes the limitations of an analysis based purely on raw data and that

Cherokee Creek Route G outperforms the other alternative routes based upon this more wholesale

analysis.38

            Further, Segment K13/K51 Landowners also support selection of Cherokee Creek Route

G.39 Segment K13/K51 Landowners argue that “an oversimplified cost, habitable structures,

paralleling equals "best meets" route' analysis fails to account for the unique circumstances present

     Id. at 11.
36
     Cherokee Creek Partners, et. al. Initial Post-Hearing Brief at 3 (Jun. 16, 2026).
37

38

 in this case and should not be the end of the inquiry here.” 40 Segment K13/K51 Landowners further

argue that route Cherokee Creek Route G “best balances the routing criteria in light of the

extraordinary facts by protecting Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park,

utilizing the superior Colorado River crossing at Link J31, crossing the San Saba River in

proximity to existing transmission infrastructure, avoiding unnecessary ESSS and critical habitat

impacts, avoiding the historic Sloan-Nored Ranch and other historic ranches discussed herein, and

performing strongly under the paralleling criteria.” 41

              Though Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve has concerns that Cherokee Creek Route G

does not use link U3 to cross the Colorado River, the alternative route is still far superior to routes

894 and route 496. Further, Cherokee Creek Route G does not use links H1 or G52 which, as has

been addressed extensively in this Reply Brief, suffer from significant cost discrepancies as well

as significant undercounting of habitable structures. While Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve

ultimately thinks route 392 is the better route selection, it agrees that selection of either Cherokee

Creek Route G is a reasonable selection that it could support.



       III.       PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT

              Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve would offer the following proposed findings of

              fact:

       1. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve is a ranch and nature preserve located in Burnet

              County, Texas.42



40
     Id. at 4.
41
     Id. at 55.
42
     Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve Exhibit 1, Noonan Direct at Bates 5.

                                                         18
        2. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve would be substantially affected by construction of

            links H1 or G52.43

       3. Construction of route 894, or any routes that utilize links H1 or G52 would impact three

            (3) additional habitable structures over what was stated by Joint Applicants. 44

       4. Construction of route 894, or any routes that utilize links H1 or G52 would prevent use of

            legacy landing zones and effectively end exotic wildlife management operations and

            support of critical medical transport operations on the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

            Preserve.45

       5. Construction of route 894, or any routes that utilize links H1 or G52 would severely impact

            the animals at the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve including a number of endangered
